title: From the Jupiter-8 to the super saw
intro: The JP-8080 is the rack version of Roland’s JP-8000, the 1996 synth that modelled analogue circuits in software and put its own new waveform beside them: the super saw, seven detuned sawtooths in one oscillator. Within a few years that sound had become the lead and pad of trance. The rack added ten voices, unison, distortion, an external input and a vocoder, the Voice Modulator.

timeline.name: Roland Jupiter-8
timeline.text: Roland’s analogue flagship: two oscillators a voice with sync and cross modulation, a 12/24 dB filter, and a split and dual keyboard. The JP-8000’s name echoes it, and so do its cross mod, its -12/-24 dB switch and its Upper and Lower parts.

timeline.name: Roland JP-8000
timeline.text: An eight-voice keyboard whose analogue voice is a DSP model, with the super saw, feedback osc, triangle mod and filtered noise on OSC 1, a ribbon, motion control and an arpeggiator. The JP-8080 contains its 64 preset performances and 128 preset patches.

timeline.name: Roland JP-8080
timeline.text: The same engine in a 2U rack or desktop unit, with ten voices, unison, distortion among the multi-effects, an external input that can replace OSC 2, the Voice Modulator (a 12-band vocoder), RPS phrases and two parts played singly, layered or split.

relatives.name: Roland Jupiter-8
relatives.text: The analogue flagship the JP-8000 was named after, with the same two-part keyboard and cross mod. This app plays it.

relatives.name: UDO Audio Super Gemini
relatives.text: A hybrid flagship whose first oscillator holds its own super-wave stack, the JP-8000’s idea in an analogue-filtered voice, with two parts split or layered. This app plays it.

relatives.name: Novation Supernova
relatives.text: A rival virtual-analogue rack synth of the same year, with more voices and parts, built on the same idea of modelling an analogue voice in DSP.

note: None of the databank’s records name the JP-8080 yet.
